opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core intuition is that if you fix the problem, you've already bounded what you can discover. Most of machine learning, and honestly most of how we've used AI for science so far, works on a static target: here's a benchmark, here's a loss function, go optimize. That's incredibly powerful, but it's fundamentally convergent. You climb a hill someone else has defined, and once you're at the top, the process stops being interesting.

If you look at the systems that seem genuinely open-ended, like biological evolution, human culture, or science itself, the problems aren't handed down from above. They co-evolve with the solutions. When a species evolves a new capability, it changes the environment for every other organism, and that creates new niches and new challenges. In science, solving one question almost always exposes three better ones you couldn't even have formulated before. The solution reshapes the problem space.

There's a nice line of work here, things like POET from Rui Wang, Jeff Clune and Ken Stanley, where environments and agents are generated together. The environments get harder just as the agents become capable of handling them, and you get these stepping stones you'd never find by aiming directly at the final objective. That's a big part of Ken's argument about objectives being deceptive. If you only pursue the goal you can see, you often miss the path that actually leads somewhere interesting.

There's also a practical side. With large language models we now have systems that can propose problems as well as solve them. They can write a new task, a new benchmark variant, or a new research hypothesis. That makes co-evolution tractable in a way it wasn't before. You can have a loop where the system generates candidate problems, filters them for being interesting, meaning learnable but not trivial and novel relative to what's in the archive, then tries to solve them, and the solutions feed back into which problems get generated next.

The hard part, and I think this is where a lot of the open research is, is defining "interesting" without smuggling in a fixed objective through the back door. If your notion of interestingness is static, you've just moved the hill. So you need some measure of novelty or learning progress that is itself relative to the current state of the archive. That's why I think problems and solutions have to evolve together. Neither one alone gives you the kind of unbounded, compounding discovery we actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response says solutions can reshape the problem space and expose new questions, but does not clearly state that innovation on a given problem may require first inventing a different problem.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss automatically discovering problem reductions or identify that capability as missing from current AI discovery systems.

r003.rationale: The response describes co-evolving environments and agents and finding stepping stones, but does not clearly say this produces more diverse stepping stones.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it is that if you fix the problem distribution up front, you've essentially put a ceiling on what the system can ever discover. Whatever benchmark or task set you hand-design, the agent will eventually saturate it, and then you're stuck. The interesting stuff, the genuinely novel stuff, tends to live just beyond the edge of what you thought to ask for.

The intuition really comes from looking at how progress happens in science or in evolution. New capabilities open up new problems that weren't even expressible before, and those new problems in turn pressure the system to develop new capabilities. It's a ratchet. Solutions create the conditions for the next generation of problems, and problems shape the search space for the next generation of solutions. If you decouple those two, you lose the ratchet.

There's also a very practical issue, which is the Goldilocks zone of difficulty. A learner only makes progress on problems that are neither trivially solved nor hopelessly out of reach. If the problem set is static, that zone drifts away from you as the agent improves. By co-evolving, you get a kind of automatic curriculum: problems that are just a bit harder than what the current population can solve are the ones that get selected for, and the solvers chase them. Things like POET from Jeff Clune and Ken Stanley's group showed this really nicely, where the environments and the agents push each other into regions neither would have reached alone.

And then with large models in the loop, this gets much more interesting, because the model can act as both the problem proposer and the solver. It can look at what's been solved, judge what would be a novel and interesting next step, and generate it. That's where I think the open-endedness angle really comes from: you're not trying to optimize toward a known target, you're trying to maintain a steady stream of learnable novelty. And you simply can't do that if one half of the system is frozen.

r001.rationale: The response says new capabilities can make new problems expressible, but does not state that innovation on a given problem may require inventing a different problem first.

r002.rationale: It does not mention automatically discovering problem reductions or whether current discovery systems have that capability built in.

r003.rationale: It describes co-evolution as a ratchet and automatic curriculum, but does not clearly say it produces more diverse stepping stones for discovery.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that if you fix the problem, you’ve already decided what counts as progress. You can get increasingly good solutions, but you’re exploring within a boundary that someone set in advance. For open-ended discovery, we’d like the system to expand that boundary—to discover useful questions as well as answers.

And those two processes depend on each other. A new solution can make a previously inaccessible problem tractable, while a new problem can expose a limitation in the solutions you already have. That creates a feedback loop: capabilities open up new challenges, and those challenges push capabilities further.

But you need some coupling between them. If problems evolve independently, they might become impossible or simply uninteresting. If solutions evolve against a fixed set of problems, they might become very specialized. The interesting regime is where new challenges are within reach, but require something meaningfully different from what the system already knows how to do.

That’s also why I wouldn’t equate open-endedness with just generating novelty. You want discoveries that become stepping stones—things that create opportunities for further discovery, even when you couldn’t have specified their eventual value at the beginning.

r001.rationale: The response describes problems and solutions enabling each other, but does not state that innovating on a given problem may require inventing a different problem first.

r002.rationale: It does not mention problem reductions or say that current AI discovery systems may lack the capability to discover them automatically.

r003.rationale: It describes co-evolution and says discoveries can become stepping stones, but does not claim that co-evolution produces more diverse stepping stones.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that what counts as an interesting problem depends on what you can already do. If you fix the task in advance, you can get better and better at that task, but you’re not necessarily creating the conditions for something genuinely new to emerge.

When problems and solutions evolve together, a new capability can open up a new set of challenges, and those challenges can create pressure for further capabilities. You get this feedback loop. Evolution is a useful analogy: organisms don’t just adapt to an environment; they change the environment and, with it, the challenges that other organisms face.

But you need some balance. If the problems become difficult too quickly, there’s no learning signal. If they stay too easy, there’s no pressure to discover anything. The interesting part is maintaining a frontier where the challenges are just within reach, while preserving enough diversity that you don’t collapse onto one narrow direction. That’s what makes the process potentially open-ended: solving a problem helps create the space of problems you might tackle next.

r001.rationale: The response says new capabilities can create new challenges, but does not state that innovation on a given problem may require inventing a different problem first.

r002.rationale: It does not mention automatically discovering problem reductions or whether current AI discovery systems have that capability built in.

r003.rationale: It describes problems and solutions creating a feedback loop, with new capabilities opening new challenges, and says preserving diversity makes the process potentially open-ended.
